docs/deployment-guide.md and CLAUDE.md — state which command is the local quality gate and what it covers, once it is green.
tests: `make test` exits 0 on a clean checkout, on both an @2x and an @3x simulator.
`make check` runs without tripping the repo's local hook.

clusters.notes:
Blunt assessment: the audit got the CI/release-pipeline half right and the engineering half wrong.

WRONG — P0-05-01. There is no arrow-head rendering bug. I rendered the control on Xcode 27.0 / iOS 26.3 and the arrow draws complete (shaft + head), and the failure text is a SIZE mismatch (`Newly-taken snapshot@(390,700) does not match reference@(260,466.67)`), which means SnapshotTesting rejected the reference before ever comparing pixels. All three reference PNGs are @2x renders (780x240 / 780x1400) being compared on @3x devices — including CI's pinned iPhone 17 Pro. The audit invented an SVG/mask/symbol-config hypothesis for a failure that never reached the pixel stage. It also missed the genuinely interesting half: the LockControl reference is visually stale because commit 05444954 (2026-07-31) changed the knob ring from `primaryText` to `accentForeground` and nobody re-recorded.

WRONG — P0-05-02. `item.detail.more` is set correctly at ItemDetailScreen.swift:302 and has never been exercised. The test dies three lines earlier at `item.tap()` with "Failed to not hittable". Acting on this finding would have produced a pointless toolbar refactor.

RIGHT but under-scoped — P0-05-03. The tutorial blocker is real, and it is the single root cause of BOTH UI tests, not just the panic-restart one. I have the proof: the exported UI-hierarchy attachment contains "Add your first item / Step 1 of 3", and the last frame of the panic test's screen recording shows "Step 2 of 3 — Check your security" over Home — i.e. the test's taps were being eaten by the scrim and were advancing the tour. Two findings collapse into one 1-hour fix in AppEnvironment.init.

MISSED — three things. (a) TutorialTooltipSnapshotTests.testClosingStepCardWithoutSkip CRASHES the app: SIGABRT, malloc "pointer being freed was not allocated", in LooxEntitlementCoordinator's synthesized isolated deinit via swift_task_deinitOnExecutorMainActorBackDeploy. A crash is worse than a mismatch and the audit did not notice it. (b) scripts/ci/select-xcode.sh hard-pins Xcode 26.5 and exits 1 here (machine has 26.6 and 27.0) — if the release runner ever updates Xcode, no tag can ship. That is the only item in this cluster that can literally stop a release. (c) `make test` runs all three test targets via the auto-generated Vaultify scheme, so the documented local gate is permanently red — which is the mechanism that let the other defects through.

OVERSTATED — the "Release compiler warnings" framing. Count is exactly right (7, verified by a clean Release compile), but they are not Release-specific: Project.swift's only per-configuration setting is APS_ENVIRONMENT, so the same 7 appear in Debug. Also, six of them are harmless reads of immutable constants; the one that actually matters is Level2BiometricKeyStore.swift:137, where a discarded OSStatus silently swallows exactly the shared-group Keychain sweep failure the code comment says the sweep exists to catch. `_ = ` is the wrong fix there.

CAUTION on P0-05-04. The release job genuinely has zero dependency on any quality run for the tagged SHA — the `release-preflight` job and its `needs:` were deleted in 200c961b, leaving a vestigial `permissions: actions: read`. But removing the snapshot and critical-UI CI jobs was a deliberate, reasoned owner decision recorded in 1d64d656 ("tripled every CI run on the self-hosted runner... The test targets stay in the repo and remain runnable locally"). Per the repo's own review rules, an audit does not get to reverse that; present the trade-off and let the owner decide. Adding a same-SHA gate to release-ios.yml is the change that does not touch the decision.

VERIFICATION CAVEAT, stated once and it applies to everything above: I could not run on the pinned Xcode 26.5 / iOS 26.5 because neither is installed here (that is NEW-2). Every empirical result is from Xcode 27.0 with an iOS 26.3 simulator. The scale mismatch, the tutorial blocker and the 7 warnings are toolchain-independent by construction; the LooxEntitlementCoordinator crash is the one finding that could plausibly be a 27.0-beta artifact and must be re-run on the pin before app code is touched.

READ-ONLY confirmed: I created and then deleted one simulator (UDID 3C5018E4-...) and wrote only to /tmp. No repository file was modified.

findings.claim: Erase Vault never even attempts to revoke Quick Links (Loox Link) — it destroys the revoke tokens instead, leaving up to 30 days of live, fetchable ciphertext that is then permanently unrevokable.
findings.evidence: AppEnvironment.swift:386-388 (inside eraseLocalState): "// Quick-link revoke tokens die with the vault; the links themselves / // expire server-side (we can't revoke without the tokens anyway). / looxLinks.records.wipe()". LooxLinkRecordStore.swift:97-102 — wipe() sets records=[] and calls KeychainStore.delete(account: "loox-link-records"), with no network call. The comment's premise is false at that moment: the tokens ARE in hand until this line runs. A working per-share revoke exists and is used elsewhere — LooxLinkService.swift:186-198 revoke(_:) -> LooxLinkAPIClient.swift:166-168 POST "/v1/shares/<id>/revoke" with body {"revoke_token": …}; server side workers/loox-link/src/index.ts:207-214 routes it and src/shares.ts:163-195 revokeShare() compares sha256(presented) against revoke_token_hash. There is NO bulk/principal revoke endpoint: index.ts only exposes /v1/health, /health/live, /health/ready, /v1/link/service-state, /v1/attestation/challenges, /v1/attestation/register, POST /v1/shares, GET /v1/shares/:id, POST /v1/shares/:id/revoke, POST /v1/short-links. TTL ceiling: LooxLinkConfig.swift:74 "static let maxExpirySeconds: UInt64 = 2_592_000 // 30 days" and ExpiryPreset.thirtyDays = 2_592_000 (LooxLinkConfig.swift:93). LooxLinkRecordStore.swift:3-6 states plainly: "The revoke token is the only credential that can kill the link server-side".
findings.realRisk: A user shares a password via a 30-day Quick Link, then taps Erase Everything (e.g. selling/returning the phone, or after a suspected compromise). The link keeps serving the encrypted snapshot for the remaining TTL to anyone holding the URL — the content key is in the URL fragment, so the recipient (or anyone the URL leaked to: chat history, clipboard manager, browser sync) still decrypts the item. Because the only revoke credential was just deleted from the Keychain, neither the user nor support can ever kill it. This is the single sharpest gap in the cluster and it is a client-only fix — no server change needed.
changeScope: Vaultify/App/AppEnvironment.swift — in eraseEverything(), before eraseLocalState() runs, capture the non-expired records from looxLinks.records and await a bounded bulk revoke; only then call eraseLocalState(). Do not leave the revoke in an unstructured Task, because eraseLocalState() wipes the tokens synchronously first (all these services are @MainActor, so a Task{} body cannot start until the current synchronous MainActor run completes — verified: CloudSyncService.swift:13, ApprovalShareService.swift:10, InviteInboxService.swift:17 are all @MainActor).

Vaultify/Features/Sharing/LooxLink/LooxLinkService.swift — add revokeAllForErase() async -> (attempted: Int, failed: [LooxLinkRecord]) modeled on RelayService.disableAllForErase() (RelayService.swift:148-156): iterate records.records.filter { !$0.isExpired }, call the existing revoke(_:), treat LooxLinkAPIError.notFound as success (already handled at LooxLinkService.swift:190-192), collect failures.

Vaultify/Features/Settings/SettingsScreen.swift — extend eraseWithRelayTeardown() (lines 47-58) so the pre-erase gate covers quick links as well as aliases, and widen the existing "Network needed" alert (lines 269-277) to name live links; the Erase Anyway fallback (line 274) stays.

Vaultify/Features/Sharing/LooxLink/LooxLinkRecordStore.swift — replace the now-wrong comment premise; optionally add wipe(keeping:) so records that failed to revoke are the only thing retained, if a retry is chosen over hard delete (call out the trade-off: retaining tokens after an 'erase' is itself residue).
tests: EraseTeardownTests.test_eraseEverything_revokesEveryLiveQuickLink_beforeTokensAreWiped — inject a fake link API, seed 3 live + 1 expired record, run the erase entry point, assert exactly the 3 live shareIds got a revoke call and that the revoke calls were observed BEFORE the record store was emptied.
EraseTeardownTests.test_quickLinkRevoke_treats404AsSuccess — API double throws LooxLinkAPIError.notFound; assert no failure is reported and the record is dropped.

EraseTeardownTests.test_eraseBlockedWhenLiveQuickLinksAndRevokeFails — API double throws URLError.notConnectedToInternet; assert the erase gate reports the blocked state (same shape as relayBlockErase) instead of silently continuing.
LooxLinkConfigTests.test_maxExpiryMatchesLongestPreset — pin ExpiryPreset.thirtyDays == maxExpirySeconds so the blast-radius window can't grow unnoticed.

findings.claim: macOS Erase Vault bypasses the relay alias teardown entirely — the fail-closed guard exists only on the iOS Settings screen.
findings.evidence: MacSettingsView.swift:179-183: ".confirmationDialog(\"Erase the entire vault?\", isPresented: $confirmErase, …) { Button(\"Erase Everything\", role: .destructive) { env.eraseEverything() } }" — a direct call, no teardown. The guard lives only in SettingsScreen.swift:47-58 eraseWithRelayTeardown(), which is the sole caller of RelayService.disableAllForErase(); grep for that symbol returns exactly two hits: the declaration (RelayService.swift:150) and SettingsScreen.swift:54. RelayService.swift:148-149 states the contract the mac path violates: "Disable every alias of this principal — the Erase-Vault teardown step. MUST succeed (durable backend ack) before a vault with active aliases is erased." Aliases are a synced plane — CloudSyncService.swift:35 "case aliases = \"VaultEmailAlias\"" — so a Mac that never created an alias still holds every alias created on iPhone in repository.aliases. MacSettingsView.swift:1 is `#if os(macOS)` and Project.swift:56 declares `.multiplatform(iOS: "17.3", macOS: "15.0")`, so this is a shipping surface, not dead code.
findings.realRisk: User erases from the Mac. Active anonymous relay aliases keep forwarding to their real inbox indefinitely, with no warning shown. Worse, eraseEverything() then drops the whole "Vault" CloudKit zone (CloudSyncService.swift:138), so the alias list is destroyed on every device — the user can no longer see or disable those aliases from anywhere in the app. Unlike the iOS path they never even get the "Erase Anyway" disclosure. Support-visible, and directly contradicts the privacy promise of the Private Email feature.
changeScope: Vaultify/App/AppEnvironment.swift — move the alias precondition out of the iOS view: add an async eraseEverything() (or a small EraseCoordinator) that performs the relay teardown itself and returns a blocked/completed outcome, so no platform can reach the raw destructive path by accident. Make the current synchronous eraseEverything() private or rename it to eraseAfterTeardown().

Vaultify/Features/Settings/SettingsScreen.swift — reduce eraseWithRelayTeardown() (lines 47-58) to a call into the shared coordinator; keep the existing "Network needed" alert (lines 269-277) as the presentation of the blocked outcome.

Vaultify/Features/Settings/MacSettingsView.swift — replace the direct env.eraseEverything() at line 180 with the same coordinator call, and add the mac equivalent of the "Network needed" / "Erase Anyway" alert.
tests: EraseTeardownTests.test_eraseWithActiveAliases_blocksWhenRelayUnreachable — relay double throws; assert the vault store, session key material and settings are untouched (this is the fail-closed invariant RelayService.swift:148 declares).
EraseTeardownTests.test_eraseWithActiveAliases_callsDisableAllExactlyOnce_thenErases — assert ordering: disableAll before any local wipe.
EraseTeardownTests.test_eraseWithNoActiveAliases_skipsRelayCall — mirrors the existing guard at SettingsScreen.swift:48 / RelayService.swift:151.

A compile-level guard is cheap here: keep exactly one non-private erase entry point so a future platform view cannot re-introduce the bypass; assert via grep in a lint/test that eraseEverything has one call site per platform view.

findings.claim: Erase Vault's remote teardown fails open: CloudKit zone/subscription deletion, approval-share revocation and inbox disarm are fire-and-forget with swallowed errors and no retry.
findings.evidence: AppEnvironment.swift:352-359 is the whole function: "func eraseEverything() { Task { [cloudSync] in await cloudSync.eraseRemote() } / Task { [approvalShare] in await approvalShare.revokeAllOwned() } / Task { [inviteInbox] in await inviteInbox.disarm() } / eraseLocalState() }". Three unstructured Tasks, none retained, none awaited, no result inspected, no UI feedback. All four participants are @MainActor (AppEnvironment.swift:6, CloudSyncService.swift:13, ApprovalShareService.swift:10, InviteInboxService.swift:17), so the Task bodies cannot begin until eraseLocalState() has fully run — the local wipe always wins the race. Errors are swallowed at every layer: CloudSyncService.swift:136-145 eraseRemote() is "_ = try? await database.modifyRecordZones(saving: [], deleting: [zone.zoneID])" then "_ = try? await database.modifySubscriptions(…)" — no result inspection at all, unlike the deliberately careful per-zone check in ApprovalShareService.swift:483-490 which does read deleteResults. ApprovalShareService.swift:522-527 revokeAllOwned() is "let names = (try? await ownedApprovalZoneNames()) ?? Self.ownedZoneNames; for zoneName in … { try? await revoke(zoneName: zoneName) }" — per-zone failures discarded. InviteInboxService.swift:173-183 disarm() uses "_ = try? await publicDB.modifyRecords(…)" and "_ = try? await publicDB.modifySubscriptions(…)". WHERE THE AUDIT OVERSTATES IT: (a) the relay/alias path is already fail-CLOSED on iOS (SettingsScreen.swift:47-58 blocks the erase and shows "Network needed", lines 269-277) — this is not a blanket fail-open design; (b) the ordering hazard is smaller than it looks for approvals — ApprovalShareService's zone registry key "approval_owner_zone_names" (ApprovalShareService.swift:45-49) is plain UserDefaults and is NOT touched by eraseLocalState() (SharingStore.wipe() at SharingStore.swift:194-197 only clears its own `shares` key), so the offline fallback list survives the local wipe intact and even survives relaunch; (c) eraseRemote() does not consult settings.iCloudSyncEnabled (only `guard Self.isConfigured`, CloudSyncService.swift:137), so eraseLocalState() setting iCloudSyncEnabled=false at AppEnvironment.swift:410 does NOT disable it; (d) CloudKit auth is the iCloud account, not vault key material, so session.resetVault() (AppEnvironment.swift:415 -> VaultSession+Recovery.swift:84-94) does not break the pending deletes. Quick links are the one thing where the ordering IS fatal — see NEW-1.
findings.realRisk: On an offline or iCloud-throttled erase, the sealed vault records + recovery envelope stay in the private "Vault" zone and every approval CKShare stays alive, so a recipient keeps their mirrored zone and the printed Emergency Kit can still resurrect the vault — and the user is told nothing, because the erase UI dismisses to onboarding regardless of outcome. If the process is killed during erase (user force-quits after the screen lands on onboarding, or the OS suspends), the Tasks are dropped mid-flight. The mitigating facts are that the approval zone registry survives in UserDefaults (a cheap retry is possible) and the ordinary sync path will not resurrect data because the local store is wiped.
changeScope: Vaultify/App/AppEnvironment.swift — replace the three unstructured Tasks at lines 353-357 with a single async teardown that awaits them (withTaskGroup over three @MainActor calls is fine here) and returns a per-step outcome; call eraseLocalState() only after that, except for the quick-link step which must run strictly first (NEW-1). Keep the existing handleRemoteSignOut() path (lines 371-380) untouched — it correctly runs eraseLocalState() alone with none of the remote teardown.

Vaultify/Services/Sync/CloudSyncService.swift — change eraseRemote() (lines 136-145) from `-> Void` to a throwing/result-returning form: inspect modifyRecordZones deleteResults the same way ApprovalShareService.revoke() does at lines 483-490 (treat .zoneNotFound / .userDeletedZone as success), and only clear savedChangeToken / SyncPushService.clearLocalFlag() when the zone delete actually succeeded.

Vaultify/Services/Sharing/ApprovalShareService.swift — make revokeAllOwned() (lines 522-527) return the zone names that failed instead of discarding them; leave the successful ones unregistered via the existing unregisterZone() at line 501 so the surviving "approval_owner_zone_names" entries are exactly the retry set.

Vaultify/Features/Settings/SettingsScreen.swift + Vaultify/Features/Settings/MacSettingsView.swift — show progress during the awaited teardown (the `erasing` state at SettingsScreen.swift:17 already exists but is only used for the relay step) and surface a partial-teardown result instead of silently landing on onboarding.

Vaultify/App/AppEnvironment.swift (retry) — on next launch, if "approval_owner_zone_names" is non-empty while settings.onboardingCompleted is false, re-run revokeAllOwned() best-effort. This is the only durable retry that is currently possible without inventing new persistence.
tests: EraseTeardownTests.test_eraseAwaitsAllRemoteSteps_beforeReportingComplete — fake cloud/approval/inbox doubles that suspend; assert the completion outcome is not delivered until all three resolve.

EraseTeardownTests.test_partialTeardownIsReported_notSwallowed — cloud double fails with CKError.networkUnavailable; assert the returned outcome names the failed step (today the error vanishes at CloudSyncService.swift:138).
EraseTeardownTests.test_zoneNotFoundCountsAsSuccess — cloud double fails with CKError.zoneNotFound; assert success, mirroring ApprovalShareService.swift:486.
EraseTeardownTests.test_approvalZoneRegistryRetainsOnlyFailedZones — two zones, one revoke throws; assert "approval_owner_zone_names" afterwards contains exactly the failed one.

EraseTeardownTests.test_remoteSignOutPathRunsNoRemoteTeardown — call handleRemoteSignOut(); assert zero cloud/approval/inbox calls (protects the AppEnvironment.swift:368-370 invariant while refactoring).

NOTE on feasibility: these must run against injected protocol doubles, not CKDatabase — CloudSyncService.swift:96-99 documents that CKContainer.init TRAPS under XCTest (isHostingUnitTests), so the teardown sequencer has to be extracted behind protocols to be testable at all. That extraction is most of the effort.

findings.claim: The Erase Vault copy says 'on this device' in all three languages while the action also destroys the shared iCloud copy and revokes every approval share — there is no this-device vs everywhere distinction anywhere in the UI.
findings.evidence: Identical dialog in both platform views — SettingsScreen.swift:278-282 and MacSettingsView.swift:179-183: title "Erase the entire vault?", message "This permanently deletes every item and key on this device. This cannot be undone." Localizable.xcstrings has all three translated and all three keep the device scoping: vi "Thao tác này xóa vĩnh viễn mọi mục và khóa trên thiết bị này. Không thể hoàn tác.", ja "この操作はこのデバイス上のすべてのアイテムと鍵を完全に削除します。元に戻せません。". What actually happens is broader: CloudSyncService.swift:138 deletes the shared "Vault" zone (which per DeviceRegistryService.swift:58,83 also holds the owner-device registry rows, and per RelayPrincipalEscrowService.swift:121-122 the relay principal escrow), and ApprovalShareService.swift:522 revokes every share this owner created. By contrast the remote sign-out path DOES distinguish, and its string proves the vocabulary exists: "Another device removed this device from the vault. Loox data on this device was erased. Your items remain in the vault." (Localizable.xcstrings; vi/ja translated). Nothing in the erase copy mentions surviving Quick Links either.
findings.realRisk: Two opposite user harms from one string. (1) Data loss by surprise: a user with iPhone + iPad + Mac reads 'on this device', erases the device they are selling, and silently loses the vault on the other two — irreversible, and the exact scenario a password manager cannot afford. (2) False comfort: someone erasing after a suspected compromise is never told that live Quick Links (up to 30 days, NEW-1) and any relay aliases (NEW-2 on Mac) keep working. Also relevant to App Review only indirectly, but it is a Data Deletion accuracy issue.

clusters.notes:
Blunt assessment of the audit's P0-06.

WHAT IT GOT RIGHT: eraseEverything() really is three unretained, unawaited Task{}s with `try?` swallowing at every layer (AppEnvironment.swift:352-359, CloudSyncService.swift:136-145, ApprovalShareService.swift:522-527, InviteInboxService.swift:173-183). No result is ever inspected or shown. That part is exactly as described.

WHAT IT OVERSTATED:
1. "Fail-open" is not the design. The relay/alias step is already fail-CLOSED on iOS: SettingsScreen.swift:47-58 blocks the erase outright, shows a "Network needed" alert, and only proceeds via an explicit "Erase Anyway" that states the consequence. Someone deliberately built the right pattern once. The bug is that it was never applied to the other three remote steps or to the Mac.
2. The ordering hazard is narrower than a blanket "local wipe destroys what remote teardown needs." I checked each dependency: ApprovalShareService's zone registry ("approval_owner_zone_names", ApprovalShareService.swift:45-49) is plain UserDefaults and is NOT wiped by eraseLocalState() — SharingStore.wipe() (SharingStore.swift:194-197) only clears its own key. eraseRemote() does not read settings.iCloudSyncEnabled (only `guard Self.isConfigured`), so setting it false at AppEnvironment.swift:410 doesn't disable it. CloudKit auth is the iCloud account, not vault key material, so session.resetVault() doesn't break the pending deletes. If the audit claimed ordering breaks all three remote steps, that's REFUTED.
3. All four types are @MainActor (verified), so the Task bodies provably cannot start until eraseLocalState() finishes. The local wipe always wins — deterministically, not racily. Worth stating precisely because it makes any fix ordering-sensitive in exactly one place: quick links.

WHAT IT MISSED — and these are bigger than the CloudKit fail-open:
- NEW-1: Quick Links are never revoked AT ALL. Not "best-effort and might fail" — zero attempt, and the revoke tokens are deleted from the Keychain in the same breath (AppEnvironment.swift:386-388, LooxLinkRecordStore.swift:97-102). Max TTL is 30 days (LooxLinkConfig.swift:74). The in-code justification "we can't revoke without the tokens anyway" is circular: the tokens are in hand until that exact line. A working per-share revoke exists on both client and server. Client-only fix. This is the finding I'd ship first.
- NEW-2: macOS erase bypasses the relay teardown entirely (MacSettingsView.swift:180 calls env.eraseEverything() raw). Aliases sync via the VaultEmailAlias plane, so a Mac holds iPhone-created aliases; erasing from the Mac leaves them forwarding AND destroys the alias list everywhere via the zone delete, making them permanently unrevokable from the app. The codebase's own comment (RelayService.swift:148-149) calls this step a MUST.
- NEW-3: the copy says "on this device" in EN/VI/JA while the action deletes the shared iCloud zone. This cuts both ways — silent multi-device data loss for the honest user, false comfort for the compromised one.

ANSWER TO Q6, PLAINLY: there is no durable retry state of any kind. No BGTaskScheduler anywhere in the repo; beginBackgroundTask appears exactly once (AppPushDelegate.swift:150) and is unrelated. What survives relaunch after an erase: the raw UserDefaults domain (resetVault only flips specific keys — VaultSession+Recovery.swift:84-94), which means ApprovalShareService's "approval_owner_zone_names" list is still there and COULD drive a free retry, though nothing reads it. What does not survive: the Quick Link revoke tokens (Keychain, deleted), the vault store, all key material, and any in-flight Task. Net: if the three Tasks don't complete before the process ends, the remote state is orphaned forever, and for quick links it's orphaned even on the happy path.

Quick View is NOT part of this problem — sessions carry a 180s create-to-approval TTL (workers/loox-quick-view/src/session-do.ts:45-46), so quickViewHistory.wipe() being local-only is harmless. I checked so it wouldn't get swept in.

findings.claim: ArtifactStore relativePath / fileURL / exportPlaintext joining lets a crafted artifact id or filename escape the artifact root.
findings.evidence: ArtifactStore.swift:58-60 `private func fileURL(for record: ArtifactRecord) -> URL { root.appending(path: record.relativePath) }`. restoreAll passes attacker bytes straight through: :314 `insertArtifact(id: payload.id, ownerItemId: payload.ownerItemId, filename: payload.filename, ...)`; :351 `relativePath: "\(id).enc"`; :354 `try envelope.write(to: fileURL(for: record), options: [.atomic, .completeFileProtection])`. The payload is unvalidated — VaultBackup.swift:349-351 returns `ArtifactPayload(id: portable.id, ownerItemId: portable.ownerItemId, filename: portable.filename, ...)` and validatedArtifacts (:323-353) checks ONLY byteCount, AEAD, plaintext length and SHA-256 — never id, ownerItemId or filename shape. exportPlaintext is worse (no forced suffix): :199-201 `let name = manifest.filename.isEmpty ? record.id : manifest.filename` / `let url = directory.appending(path: name)` / `try data.write(to: url, ...)`. I ran the real Foundation APIs: `URL.appending(path:)` and `appendingPathComponent(_:)` both pass `..` through verbatim and the kernel resolves it — `root.appending(path: "../Library/Preferences/x.plist#.enc")` from root `<c>/Artifacts-v2` physically wrote to `<c>/Library/Preferences/x.plist#.enc` (escaped root = true), and a crafted manifest filename `../../../Library/Preferences/pwned.plist` from `<c>/tmp/artifact-exports/<uuid>/` physically wrote to `<c>/Library/Preferences/pwned.plist`. Only percent-encoded `..%2F` is inert. Reachability of the export leg is complete: AttachmentFieldRow.swift:75-81 resolves `env.artifactStore.record(id: meta.id)` from a `.fileRef` field the backup also supplies, then calls `exportPlaintext(record)` on tap. Escaped files are invisible to the janitor: reconcile (:265-271) enumerates only `root`, and eraseAll (:242) removes only `root`.
findings.realRisk: The audit's gating premise is backwards and should not be used to downgrade this. The attacker AUTHORS the backup, so they choose the passphrase and hand it to the victim ("here's the team vault, password is X"). The bar is not "knows your passphrase" — it is "gets you to import a .vaultify file", which is the exact threat model an import feature exists to survive. Concretely: (a) import alone, zero further taps, writes attacker-chosen `.enc` files anywhere in the App Group / app container the app can write; (b) one tap on the attachment writes fully attacker-chosen bytes to a fully attacker-chosen path with NO suffix constraint — inside the app container that reaches Library/Preferences (the UserDefaults plist backing biometricUnlockEnabled / crashReportingEnabled / iCloudSyncEnabled) and Library/Application Support (the SharedConfig fallback store location). Not RCE and not vault-key compromise — the App Group container path is unguessable and the id leg is `.enc`-suffixed — but it is arbitrary write/overwrite inside a password manager's own sandbox. (c) The quieter certain harm: escaped `.enc` files are never swept by reconcile() and survive "Erase Vault", so a factory-reset vault silently retains planted encrypted files.

findings.claim: KdfParams are decoded from the backup file and fed to Argon2 without clamping; artifact id / ownerItemId / filename are not validated.
findings.evidence: VaultBackup.swift:269-272 `let backup = try JSONDecoder().decode(EncryptedBackup.self, from: data)` then `KeyHierarchy.deriveKEK(passphrase: passphrase, salt: Array(backup.salt), params: backup.kdf)`. KeyHierarchy.swift:17-19 forwards `params` unchanged to `Argon2.deriveRaw`, which at Argon2.swift:28-33 passes `params.timeCost, params.memoryCostKiB, params.parallelism` straight into `argon2id_hash_raw`. KdfParams.swift:6-12 has no validating initializer, no `init(from:)`, and no clamp helper — the three UInt32s are raw Codable properties. The vendored C accepts the whole range: argon2.h:61-72 `ARGON2_MAX_MEMORY = min(0xFFFFFFFF, 1<<32)` KiB and `ARGON2_MAX_TIME UINT32_C(0xFFFFFFFF)`. Absurd memory does fail safely (core.c:89-109 returns ARGON2_MEMORY_ALLOCATION_ERROR when malloc fails) — but the dangerous band is the one that ALLOCATES: `memoryCostKiB = 2_000_000` (~2 GiB) mallocs successfully and is then fully touched, blowing past jetsam. `timeCost = 0xFFFFFFFF` at m=64MiB is ~4 years of CPU with no cancellation path — ImportView.swift:135-152 `decrypt` sets `working = true`, awaits the detached task, and offers no cancel; the only UI is `.overlay { if working { ProgressView() } }` at :92. Artifact id/ownerItemId/filename validation: confirmed absent, see P1-03 evidence.
findings.realRisk: Opening an attacker-supplied .vaultify and tapping Decrypt kills the app via jetsam (memory band) or wedges it in a permanent spinner with a pegged core, thermal throttle and battery drain (time band). Recoverable by force-quitting and not re-importing, so it is denial-of-service, not compromise — EXCEPT via the Level-2 path (NEW-1) where the hostile params get persisted. The salt is also unvalidated: an empty backup.salt makes Argon2 return ARGON2_SALT_TOO_SHORT, which surfaces as ImportView.swift:149 "Couldn't decrypt, check the password." — a wrong but harmless message.
changeScope: /Users/bervion/Developer/Projects/mobile/ios/Vaultify/VaultifyCore/Crypto/KdfParams.swift — add `static let maxMemoryCostKiB: UInt32 = 256 * 1024`, `maxTimeCost: UInt32 = 10`, `maxParallelism: UInt32 = 8`, matching floors (OWASP 19 MiB / t>=1 / p>=1), plus a `var isWithinPolicy: Bool` and a validating `init(from decoder:)` that throws DecodingError.dataCorrupted when any value is out of band — so every wire surface that decodes KdfParams (backup envelope AND Level2Wrap) is covered by one change

findings.claim: A malicious backup's Level2Wrap.kdf is persisted verbatim into this device's key bundle, turning the transient import DoS of P1-02 into a permanent, reboot-surviving denial of the Extra Password — and installs an Extra Password the user can never remove.
findings.evidence: ImportView.swift:193-196 `env.session.adoptLevel2WrapIfAbsent(wrappedL2SK: level2.wrappedL2SK, salt: level2.salt, kdf: level2.kdf)` with `level2` coming straight off the wire (VaultBackup.swift:114-118 `struct Level2Wrap { var wrappedL2SK: Data; var salt: Data; var kdf: KdfParams }`, decoded inside PortableVaultPayload with zero validation). VaultSession+Level2.swift:116-124 `level2AdoptedBundle` does `updated.l2Kdf = kdf` and :106 `try? updated.save()` — the attacker's KdfParams are now on disk in the key bundle. Every later unlock reads them back: :44-49 `guard let bundle = VaultKeyBundle.load(), let wrapped = bundle.wrappedL2SK, let salt = bundle.l2Salt, let kdf = bundle.l2Kdf ... Self.unwrap(wrapped: wrapped, password: password, salt: Array(salt), params: kdf)`. Compounding it, the adopted wrap is unremovable: Level2SettingsView.swift:119 `mode = env.session.hasLevel2 ? .overview : .setup` hides setup, :225 routes to `.turnOff`, and :308-311 `case .turnOff: try await env.session.unlockLevel2(password: current)` requires the FOREIGN password before :347 `env.session.removeLevel2Wrap()` is ever reached.
findings.realRisk: Import once and the device's Extra Password is permanently broken: every reveal of a protected field runs a 2 GiB or 4-year Argon2 with the app's own bundle as the trigger — no attacker file needed again. The AutoFill extension is the sharper edge; KdfParams.swift:19-26 documents that the extension already halves memory to 32 MiB specifically to survive its tight jetsam budget, so a planted 256 MiB+ profile terminates the credential UI. And because turn-off demands the foreign password, the user cannot undo it — the only exit is Erase Vault. This also fires on the benign path: importing a friend's or colleague's backup silently installs their Extra Password on a device that had none.

findings.claim: adoptLevel2WrapIfAbsent's never-overwrite semantics mean importing into a vault that already has a different L2 wrap silently strands the restored protected fields.
findings.evidence: VaultSession+Level2.swift:118 `guard base.wrappedL2SK == nil else { return nil }` — the documented never-overwrite rule (:96-100). ImportView.swift:193-196 calls it and ignores the outcome entirely; the very next statement is :197 `AnalyticsEngine.shared.log(.vaultImported(...))` followed by `Haptics.success(); dismiss()`. So a restore into a vault that already has an Extra Password reports unqualified success while every `guard2 == true` field it just wrote is ciphertext under the SOURCE device's L2SK. The failure surfaces only much later and unhelpfully: ProtectedFieldRow.swift:174-181 `if let text = try? SecretGuard.openLevel2(field.value, l2Key: key) { ... } else { error = appString("Couldn't decrypt this field.") }` — a generic message with no cause and no recovery path. The comment at :98-100 ("fields sealed under a DIFFERENT L2SK stay unreadable either way") is technically true and the guard is the right call; what is missing is telling the user. Confirmed untested: Level2BackupAndMaskingTests.swift covers only round-trip, no-level2 compat, CSV masking, subtitle masking and TOTP masking — nothing about a colliding wrap. The mirror-image failure (adopting onto a device with NO wrap) is NEW-1.
findings.realRisk: Two silent-data-loss shapes for ordinary users, no attacker required. (1) User has an Extra Password on device B, restores their device-A backup: every protected field imports as permanently unopenable ciphertext, reported as a successful import, discovered days later as "Couldn't decrypt this field." with no explanation. (2) User has no Extra Password and imports someone else's backup: NEW-1's unremovable foreign wrap. Both are exactly the class of failure a password manager cannot ship — the backup is the thing users trust when everything else is gone.

findings.claim: ImportView uses unbounded Data(contentsOf:) and performs a multi-step non-atomic restore.
findings.evidence: Both facts are real; the audit's severity ranking is inverted. Unbounded read — ImportView.swift:115 `guard let data = try? Data(contentsOf: url) else` with no size pre-check and no `.mappedIfSafe`, inside `handle(_:)` which is the MainActor fileImporter completion (:93-97). Non-atomic restore — performImport (:155-205) is four independently-committing phases: :177 `try env.repository.addAll(itemsToAdd)` (VaultRepository.swift:456-457 does its own `try store.context.save()` + `reload()`), :179 `try env.artifactStore.restoreAll(parsedArtifacts)` (its own save at ArtifactStore.swift:320, with real all-or-nothing rollback at :321-326 — this phase is the well-built one), :182-192 a bare `for passkey in parsedPasskeys { _ = try vault.save(passkey, key: key) }` loop with no rollback, and only then :193-196 the Level-2 adoption. The single `catch` at :201-204 sets a string and rolls back nothing. Ordering is the actual defect, not the loop: putting the L2 adoption LAST means any throw in the passkey loop leaves items and artifacts committed with the wrap unadopted, which is exactly P1-05's permanent-ciphertext outcome. Retry is only partly safe — `parsed` is not cleared so the user can press Import again, ArtifactRecord/ItemRecord both carry `@Attribute(.unique) var id` so re-insert upserts rather than duplicating, and restoreAll skips live same-id artifacts (:312-313). Mitigating the unbounded read: `allowsMultipleSelection: false` and the source is the user's own Files picker, so this is a self-inflicted memory spike, not an attack surface — the real cost is the synchronous main-thread read of a non-materialized iCloud Drive file, which is a watchdog risk.
findings.realRisk: Unbounded read: picking a multi-GB file freezes the UI during the read and can jetsam the app, or hangs the main thread while iCloud Drive materializes the file. Annoying, self-inflicted, no data loss. Non-atomic restore: a throw in the passkey loop produces a half-restored vault whose protected fields are permanently unopenable because the L2 wrap never got adopted, behind the message "Import failed before all records could be saved." — which does not tell the user that a retry is both safe and necessary.

findings.claim: ExportView uses fixed temp filenames with questionable protection and no cleanup.
findings.evidence: ExportView.swift:175-179 `let url = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appendingPathComponent(name); try data.write(to: url, options: .completeFileProtection)` with fixed names `"loox-backup.vaultify"` (:162) and `"loox-export.csv"` (:164). Correcting the audit on two points: file protection IS `.completeFileProtection`, and the fixed name is arguably right — it overwrites rather than accumulating. The genuine gap is cleanup: grepping the whole tree for `loox-export`/`loox-backup` returns only these two write sites — nothing ever deletes them. ArtifactStore.cleanupTempExports (:207-209) removes only `tmp/artifact-exports`, and VaultifyApp.swift:183 calls only that. So an unencrypted CSV containing every password persists in `<app>/tmp/` indefinitely across launches. Mitigating: `tmp/` is excluded from device backups, and .completeFileProtection means it is unreadable while the device is locked.

Given the product's own copy tells the user "Delete it as soon as you're done" (:100), the app not honoring that itself is a credibility gap as much as a security one.

findings.claim: No VersionedSchema or SchemaMigrationPlan exists anywhere; v1.50.0 adds a new SwiftData entity and the container failure path is an unrecoverable fatalError that also interpolates the store path into a Crashlytics-uploaded message.
findings.evidence: Migration plumbing: grepping the tree for VersionedSchema / SchemaMigrationPlan / MigrationStage returns zero implementations — the only hit is a comment at IconResolver.swift:27 ("`VersionedSchema` in this project, so an added column would be its own migration"). VaultStore.swift:25-39 constructs a bare `ModelContainer(for: ItemRecord.self, ..., ArtifactRecord.self, configurations: configuration)` with no migration plan, so SwiftData falls back to implicit lightweight migration. What changed v1.49.1 -> v1.50.0 (git diff --stat over VaultifyCore/Store): exactly two files — ArtifactRecord.swift (new, +75) and VaultStore.swift (+25, registering it at :38 and deleting it in eraseAll at :53). No existing entity gained or lost a column; ItemRecord.swift is untouched. The Models/ changes in that range (VaultItem.swift, DynamicField.swift, ItemSemantics.swift, DetailValuePresentation.swift, QuarantinedRecord.swift) are Codable structs sealed inside the blob, not SwiftData columns — DynamicField.swift's new init(from:)/encode(to:) at the v1.50.0 diff explicitly preserves unknown kinds via `unknownKindRaw`, so the wire is forward-compatible by design. Adding one standalone entity is the additive case lightweight migration handles, so the v1.49.1 -> v1.50.0 hop is genuinely low risk. The real defect is the failure handling: VaultStore.swift:13-14 `do { container = try Self.makeContainer(inMemory: inMemory) } catch { fatalError("Failed to initialise vault store: \(error)") }`. CLAUDE.md's crash-reporting contract states both "Never log an interpolated Error: Loox errors can embed record ids, CloudKit zone/share names and file URLs" and "precondition/fatalError MESSAGES are uploaded. Do not interpolate paths or filenames." A Core Data store-load NSError carries NSFilePath / NSURL for the store in its userInfo, and `\(error)` renders it.
findings.realRisk: Two things. (1) If any future schema change is not lightweight-migratable — a renamed or retyped column, a new unique constraint on an existing entity, an entity split — the app hard-crashes at launch for every user with an existing vault, with no recovery UI, no backup prompt, and no way back to the previous version from TestFlight or the App Store. There is no plan file to catch that at review time, so it depends entirely on someone remembering. (2) Today, in shipping code, a container failure uploads the App Group store path to Crashlytics, which is precisely what the project's own privacy contract forbids and is the kind of thing that undermines the privacy-manifest declaration. Neither is triggered by the v1.50.0 change itself — the ArtifactRecord addition is safe — so this is not a release blocker, but the fatalError message is a one-line fix that should go out now.

clusters.notes:
Where the audit was wrong or soft:

1. THE THREAT-MODEL FRAMING ON P1-03 IS BACKWARDS, and it matters more than any single finding. The task told me to factor in that "they must know the backup passphrase." That premise is inverted. The attacker AUTHORS the malicious backup, therefore the attacker CHOOSES the passphrase and hands it to the victim along with the file ("here's the shared team vault, password is X"; "import this to migrate from LastPass"). The victim's own passphrase is never involved. The bar is not cryptographic — it is "get a user to import a file," which is the single thing the import feature exists to do. Do not let that framing downgrade the fix priority.

2. P1-03 is CONFIRMED empirically, not by reading. I ran the real Foundation APIs against a real filesystem and physically wrote files outside both the artifact root and the temp-export directory. Definitively: `URL.appending(path:)` and `appendingPathComponent(_:)` behave IDENTICALLY here — neither normalizes nor rejects `..`; the string is passed through and the kernel resolves it at write time. Swapping one for the other fixes nothing. Only a `standardizedFileURL` prefix containment check does. Percent-encoded `..%2F` is inert, so encoding is not the attack.

3. The audit understated P1-03's blast radius in one direction and overstated it in another. Overstated: the id-based leg always appends `.enc`, so `Vault.store` and `vault-keybundle.json` cannot be clobbered through it, and the App Group container's random UUID path makes it unguessable from the app container — this is not vault-key compromise. Understated: `exportPlaintext` has NO forced suffix, giving full filename AND full content control, and the whole chain is reachable (AttachmentFieldRow.swift:75-81 resolves the record from a `.fileRef` field the same backup supplies). Also missed entirely: escaped `.enc` files are invisible to `reconcile()` (enumerates only `root`) and survive `eraseAll()` (removes only `root`), so "Erase Vault" does not erase them.

4. P1-04 is partly wrong. File protection is already `.completeFileProtection`, and the fixed filename is a mild positive (overwrite beats accumulate). The real defect is that nothing ever deletes the file — a plaintext CSV of every password sits in tmp/ indefinitely while the app's own copy tells the user to delete it promptly.

5. P1-01's two halves are misweighted. The unbounded `Data(contentsOf:)` is close to a non-issue — single-selection, user's own Files picker, self-inflicted; the interesting part is that it runs synchronously on MainActor and can hang on a non-materialized iCloud file. The non-atomic restore is the real bug, and specifically the ORDERING: the Level-2 wrap is adopted LAST, so any earlier failure permanently strands the sealed fields. Also worth noting the audit missed that `restoreAll` is the one phase that IS properly transactional (real rollback at ArtifactStore.swift:321-326) — credit where due.

6. Three things the audit missed, two of which I would rank above some of what it filed:
   - NEW-1 (the worst): the malicious KdfParams don't just cause a transient import DoS, they get PERSISTED into the device key bundle via `adoptLevel2WrapIfAbsent`, permanently breaking the Extra Password including in the jetsam-constrained AutoFill extension — and the adopted wrap is unremovable because turn-off requires the foreign password (Level2SettingsView.swift:308-311 gates on `unlockLevel2` before `removeLevel2Wrap`). One fix (a validating KdfParams decoder) closes both P1-02 and NEW-1, which is why P1-02 is only S effort.
   - NEW-2: encrypted export materializes every artifact plaintext at once on the main actor and then triples it through seal + base64 + seal. Ten 20 MiB attachments is a jetsam kill. This is the highest-probability real-user failure in the whole cluster and it has nothing to do with attackers.
   - NEW-3: `fatalError("Failed to initialise vault store: \(error)")` interpolates a Core Data NSError whose userInfo carries the store path, into a message CLAUDE.md explicitly says is uploaded to Crashlytics and must not contain paths. Live privacy-contract violation in shipping code, one-line fix.

7. On the migration question specifically, the honest answer is reassuring: v1.49.1 -> v1.50.0 adds exactly one standalone entity (ArtifactRecord) and changes zero existing columns — the additive case implicit lightweight migration handles. I would not block on it. The risk is structural, not present-tense: with no VersionedSchema anywhere, the first non-lightweight change ships as a launch crash for every existing user with a `fatalError` and no recovery path. Add the empty migration plan now while it costs nothing.

8. Test coverage gap worth naming: `ArtifactStoreTests` and `VaultBackupV2Tests` are thorough on the crypto (wrong hash, truncated blob, wrong declared length all abort correctly) but contain zero adversarial tests on IDENTIFIERS and PATHS. The suites validate what the bytes say and never what the names say — which is exactly the seam P1-03 lives in.

The guard is the ONLY exit for an empty string, so no event is published. SearchScreen.swift:71-77 consumes only `.query`: `if case .query(let q) = entry { search = q; suppressFocus = true; uiState.searchEntry = .normal }` — nothing else writes `search` after mount (SearchScreen.swift:22 `@State private var search = ""`). For a password manager this is a privacy-visible stale surface: item titles for a query the user explicitly erased remain on screen.

clusters.notes:
Blunt assessment of the audit report.

WHAT IT GOT RIGHT
- P1-07 is real and I confirmed the exact mechanism. The `guard !query.isEmpty else { return }` at VaultSidebarView.swift:70 is the whole bug. The audit actually UNDERSTATED it: VaultSidebarList.swift:50 filters `.search` out of the sidebar rows, so this field is the only way in or out of the Search detail. There is no second affordance to recover with.
- P1-09's direction of concern is right, but the framing is wrong. See below.

WHAT IT GOT WRONG OR OVERSTATED
- P1-08 "blocks submission" is not supported. `UIRequiresFullScreen` is absent, there is no `~ipad` variant, and `UIInterfaceOrientationPortraitUpsideDown` is missing — all three facts confirmed. But iPad support (TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY 1,2) landed at 78fb56c0 on 2026-07-28 and the repo has since shipped v1.43.1 through v1.50.0 at build 78 with this exact Info.plist. The historical ITMS-90474 iPad-multitasking orientation rejection is not firing. It is a genuine rotation UX defect worth an S-effort fix, not a release gate. Do not let a plausible-sounding App Store claim buy priority it has not earned.
- P1-09 as written implies a broken promise. The code never promised nav depth survives — AdaptiveRootView.swift:7-9 and UIStateStore.swift:31-34 both scope the guarantee to SELECTION, and selection genuinely does survive (I traced reconcileSelection and both mirrors). The real defect is narrower and one-directional: compact pushes go to UIKit (AppNavigator) and never touch the shared paths, so compact→regular loses depth, while regular→compact restores it. Fixing it properly is L, not a quick patch, and it is lower value than NEW-3 and NEW-4 below.

WHAT THE AUDIT MISSED — and these are the ones that matter
- NEW-4 is the biggest thing in this cluster and it is not an iPad issue at all. AdaptiveRootView keys only off `horizontalSizeClass`, and there is no orientation lock and no idiom check anywhere in the app (grep for supportedInterfaceOrientations/UIInterfaceOrientationMask/userInterfaceIdiom over Vaultify/ and VaultifyCore/ returns nothing). Plus/Max-class iPhones report regular horizontal size class in landscape, so a Pro Max user rotating the phone gets the iPad sidebar shell: no tab bar, a pinned 200-320pt sidebar on a compact-height screen, nil navigator so pushes change shape, and the P1-07 search bug as the only search entry point. The two-line fix is to require regular height as well.
- NEW-3 is silent data loss. ItemEditorScreen.swift:282-292 clears `uiState.editorDraft` and sweeps staged attachments from `onDisappear`, which fires on an involuntary teardown just as readily as on a real close. `restoredDraft` — the only re-presentation path (VaultShellBehaviors.swift:66) — is written solely by the one-shot cold-launch `restore()`. So an iPad window resize mid-edit deletes typed secret material with no recovery. That should gate the iPad launch far more than the orientation key does.
- NEW-1: `handleEntry()` guards on `selectedTab`, which the sidebar sets only indirectly via a separate `.onChange`. Parent-onChange vs newly-mounted-child-onAppear ordering is not guaranteed, so the first keystroke can be dropped. It costs nothing to fix inside the P1-07 change; if you fix P1-07 without also setting `selectedTab` in the same mutation, you leave the race in place.
- NEW-2: `FlushSearchHeaderChrome` (SearchScreen.swift:419-434) hides the nav bar on iOS 26 with no size-class check, justified by a tab-bar search field that only exists in the compact shell. In the iPad sidebar detail there is no tab bar. This needs a physical iPadOS 26 check before sizing — it is the one claim here I could not fully settle by reading — but the code fact is unambiguous and the fix is one environment read.
- NEW-6: no test target can even target an iPad (all three declare `destinations: [.iPhone]`), CI pins a single "iPhone 17 Pro" simulator, and VaultifySnapshotTests and VaultifyUITests are never invoked by any workflow despite the Vaultify-Quality scheme listing them. Every finding above lives in untested territory.

SUGGESTED ORDER
NEW-4 and NEW-1 + P1-07 first (all S/M, all high value, NEW-1 rides along free). Then NEW-3. Then P1-08 (S, cheap, do it). NEW-2 after a device check. NEW-5 is a bounded copy sweep — 12 strings times three languages. P1-09 and NEW-6 are the two that deserve their own planned work rather than being squeezed into this release.

ONE THING I COULD NOT VERIFY LOCALLY
Whether Plus/Max-class iPhones report regular horizontal size class in landscape on the current OS. This is long-standing Apple behavior and the reason system apps split on those devices, but NEW-4's severity rests on it — confirm on a device before the fix lands, since the fix itself (require regular height) is correct either way.

clusters.notes:
ID mapping: the brief gave one cluster label ("P1-10, P2 UI") and an 8-item verify list, so I numbered item 1 as P1-10a/b/c (three genuinely separate defects with three separate fixes) and items 2-8 as P2-UI-2 … P2-UI-8, matching your list order. NEW-1 and NEW-2 are defects the audit missed in the same files.

What the audit got WRONG:

1. Item 6 (AutoFill DS violations) is the big miss — it is not a violation at all, it is an architectural impossibility, and the audit apparently did not open Project.swift. The appex sources are `["VaultifyAutoFill/**", "VaultifyCore/**"]` (Project.swift:221): no VaultIcon, no Icons, no themedForeground, no Space/Radius/Metric. Its resources (Project.swift:225-232) include exactly one asset catalog, VaultifyCore/SharedAssets.xcassets, which contains exactly one entry — BrandLogo.imageset. Zero Polaris glyphs ship in the extension, so `Image(vaultIcon:)` there would render blank. UnlockGate.swift:80-82 and :103-104 say this in comments. Filing it as a fixable violation would have sent someone on a multi-day bundle refactor for a screen iOS draws inside its own system sheet. I also checked every SF symbol the appex uses against VaultifyTests/Fixtures/sf-symbols-ios-17-3.txt — all present, no blank-render risk — and OneTimeCodeView.swift has no SF symbols whatsoever, so naming it was wrong.

2. The raw-color half of item 6 is also wrong on its own terms. `.primary`/`.secondary`/`.red` in the appex sit on system List/Form chrome. design-guidelines.md:24 scopes its ban to "custom themed surfaces". System semantic colors on system surfaces are the correct choice, not a defect.

3. Item 5 half-refuted: LargeTypeView.swift:159's 0.5 is on a SINGLE character in an adaptive 46pt grid cell whose font is already `@ScaledMetric` — clamping it to 0.7 would clip wide glyphs at AX5. Only LooxHubScreen.swift:117 (0.65) is a real violation, and it is minor. The audit also missed EmergencyKitPDFPage.swift:79 (0.4), which is correctly exempt as off-screen PDF composition.

4. Item 2 overstated: EditorFieldRow DOES read accessibilityReduceTransparency (line 450) — it just doesn't reach a solid. And SwiftUI Material already degrades to near-opaque under Reduce Transparency at the UIKit level, so nothing becomes unreadable. This is consistency debt, not an accessibility failure.

5. Wrong path given for CopyToastOverlay — it is at Vaultify/Features/Components/, not DesignSystem/Components/.

6. Item 1 was filed as one finding but is three unrelated defects with three unrelated fixes, and the audit missed the most serious one entirely: the app-level Reduce Motion toggle is DEAD. It reaches only `\.meshAnimated`, consumed only by the wallpaper engine, which `WallpaperFeature.decorativeEnabled = false` turns off. That is a shipped setting that does nothing, and it is the single highest-value item in this cluster.

7. Item 3 was under-scoped: WallpaperGalleryView.swift:84-90 has the identical missing-.isSelected bug (not surfaced today, but it will ship the bug if wallpapers are re-enabled).

What the audit got RIGHT and I'd prioritize: P2-UI-8 (Watchtower empty state, real AX dead-end on the Security tab's first-run screen), P2-UI-3 (VoiceOver cannot determine the active theme — this one is a plain a11y failure), P2-UI-4 (three sub-44pt targets, one of them the Emergency-Kit restore escape hatch), and NEW-1 (English "Untitled" leaking into VI/JA in 9 places while 6 sibling call sites do it correctly — the app contradicts itself within one session).

On blocksSubmission: I set every finding to false, deliberately. None of these are things App Review will hit. The dead Reduce Motion toggle is arguably guideline 2.1 ("features that don't work") but a reviewer will never find it. The Watchtower AX5 clipping is the only one a thorough accessibility-minded reviewer could stumble into. If the release gate is "Apple will reject", this whole cluster is clear; if the gate is the project's own design-dna-standard.md acceptance bar, P2-UI-3, P2-UI-4, P2-UI-8 and NEW-1 all fail it explicitly and by the doc's own wording.

Two decisions that need the owner, not me:
- P1-10a: wiring the app Reduce Motion setting through (M) vs deleting the toggle (S). Deleting removes a shipped user-facing setting — per the repo's review rules that is not mine to silently undo.
- HomeScreen.swift:703-704 carries an explicit comment rejecting a 44pt frame on layout grounds. I judged the objection answerable (the layout-neutral padded-hit-area technique DNA rule 6 itself prescribes), not a standing owner decision to preserve — but flag it if that comment records a call I can't see in the file.

Unresolved: I could not compile or run anything (read-only), so all layout-overflow numbers in P2-UI-8 are arithmetic from the token values, not measured. Worth one snapshot run before committing to the fix shape.

findings.claim: /terms and /privacy 404; permanent redirects to /policies/terms and /policies/privacy are needed and must work on the Cloudflare/OpenNext deployment.
findings.evidence:
Live probe: `curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'` → /terms 404, /privacy 404, /policies/terms 200, /policies/privacy 200, /vi/policies/privacy 200. No such routes exist: the only policy route is /Users/bervion/Developer/Projects/frontend/looxpassword/src/app/[locale]/policies/[slug]/page.tsx backed by content/policies/{en,vi}/{privacy,terms,security}.mdx. The consumer is the iOS paywall: /Users/bervion/Developer/Projects/mobile/ios/Vaultify/VaultifyCore/Subscription/LooxMembership.swift:21-22 `static let termsURL = URL(string: "https://looxpassword.com/terms")!` / `privacyURL = .../privacy`, rendered at Vaultify/Features/Subscription/LooxAcquisitionPaywallView.swift:189-190 `Link("Terms of Use", destination: LooxMembership.termsURL)` / `Link("Privacy Policy", ...)`. LooxMembership.swift:19-20 states the requirement itself: "Both pages are a §12 launch gate — they must resolve before `purchasesEnabled` ever flips." And LooxMembership.swift:12-14 says beta environments — "TestFlight, App Review, Xcode/StoreKit-config runs — get the surfaces early", so an App Review build shows the paywall with two dead links even though `launchEnabled = false`.

(Workers, KV/D1, Email Routing, edge logs), and the HIBP range API; (7) international transfers + SCCs; (8) RETENTION with real numbers: Loox Link max TTL 30 days — VaultifyCore-side cap `case thirtyDays = 2_592_000` at Vaultify/Features/Sharing/LooxLink/LooxLinkConfig.swift:93 and server-side "Enforce `expires_in_seconds` ≤ 30 days" at docs/fe-cloudflare-spec.md:89 and :224, with docs/fe-cloudflare-spec.md:264 "Retention: Expired (delete immediately after expiry), Revoked (keep 30 days, then delete)" — note docs/fe-cloudflare-spec.md:42 flags cron cleanup as maintenance-only, and the claims table in docs/seo-content-plan.md marks "Permanently deleted" as ❌ do-not-use because cleanup was not enabled; also state the GA4 retention window, the Crashlytics 90-day window, Quick View session TTL, and that the favicon cache is device-local; (9) children/age statement aligned to the App Store age rating; (10) rights — access, deletion, portability, objection, withdrawal of consent — pointing at the concrete in-app switches (analytics, crash reporting, website icons, iCloud sync, breach checks) plus a CCPA "we do not sell or share" line; (11) security summary + breach notification; (12) change-notification method; (13) contact + right to complain to a supervisory authority.

clusters.notes:
Blunt assessment of the audit framing.

WHAT THE AUDIT GOT RIGHT: every one of the six cluster items is real. /terms and /privacy genuinely 404 in production right now (I curled them). The policies genuinely are self-labelled "starter template" placeholders, live, in both languages, wearing a "Last updated 1 June 2026" chip. The privacy-claim rot is real and worse than "needs rewording" in two places.

WHAT THE AUDIT UNDERSTATED — three things.

1. It framed /terms and /privacy as a route-contract nicety. It is a hard gate that the iOS codebase itself already declared. VaultifyCore/Subscription/LooxMembership.swift:19-20 says verbatim: "Both pages are a §12 launch gate — they must resolve before `purchasesEnabled` ever flips." And the paywall is NOT dark in review: LooxMembership.swift:12-14 documents that TestFlight and App Review get purchase surfaces early via `AppTransaction.environment != .production`, so a reviewer sees the paywall with two 404 links even though `launchEnabled = false`. That flips P0-01 from S-effort hygiene to submission-blocking.

2. The single most legally exposed item is not in the policy — it is src/components/home-compare.tsx:13, where CMP row 7 renders a ✓ for "No analytics or tracking SDKs" against six NAMED competitors (Apple Passwords, 1Password, Bitwarden, Proton Pass, Dashlane, LastPass, home-compare.tsx:17) while the app ships Firebase Analytics and Crashlytics enabled by default (SettingsStore.swift:238-239) with GoogleService-Info.plist present. That is false comparative advertising against named rivals, not just loose copy.

3. The audit did not look at the existing guardrail. scripts/claims-gate.sh runs on every release (deploy-marketing.sh:29) and reports "✅ claims gate passed" today — while a phrase in its own FORBIDDEN list, "no password rotation required" (claims-gate.sh:13), is live at /blog/share-access-not-secrets (I fetched it, normalised whitespace, confirmed present). It misses it because line 19 only fetches "/" and "/vi". A gate that reports green over live violations is the reason this drifted; fixing that one line is the highest leverage change in the whole cluster and costs about ten minutes.

WHAT I REFUTED / QUALIFIED.

- "Is there a support URL, contact route, and a public HTTPS test form" — PARTIALLY. /support and /contact are live and 200 in both locales, footer-linked, with real mailto addresses; App Store Connect's Support URL requirement is satisfiable today. There is no working form, and never was one by design (contact-form.tsx doc comment lines 6-10 says so) — but the actual defect is contact-form.tsx:28-29 asserting success unconditionally after a mailto navigation that can silently no-op. Loox has no accounts, so App Review needs no demo credentials; the "test form" concern does not apply the way it does for account-based apps.

- On the redirect mechanism, I did not guess. I read the installed adapter: @opennextjs/aws@4.0.2 dist/core/routingHandler.js:85 runs handleRedirects(RoutesManifest.redirects) BEFORE handleMiddleware at line 92, and matcher.js:242-263 emits 308. So next.config redirects DO work on this deployment — the audit's implied worry that only middleware works is unfounded. I still recommend middleware, because src/middleware.ts:10-17 already does exactly this for /open and /o and is proven live (302), and because it keeps one routing surface instead of two. _redirects is genuinely wrong here: wrangler.jsonc:6 sets main to the Worker, so routing is the Worker's job, and a public/_redirects would also be fetchable at /_redirects and would not fire under next dev. The sibling invite/wrangler.jsonc:5 comment about _redirects applies to an assets-only site and does not transfer.

- localePrefix 'as-needed' is a real trap the audit did not name: /vi/terms needs its own rule or it falls through to [locale]/not-found.tsx. Generate the alias table from routing.locales, not by hand, so the ja work in P0-02 does not have to revisit middleware.

WHAT I FOUND THAT THE AUDIT MISSED: NEW-1 through NEW-4 above — the false-green claims gate, the false success state in the contact form, the placeholder policies being explicitly sitemapped and index:true, and the privacy policy describing an "Account identifier tied to your Apple ID" that contradicts "No account" on five separate homepage strings while omitting the two identifiers that genuinely exist server-side (relay destination inbox, entitlement record).

ONE ITEM OUTSIDE THIS CLUSTER, flagged because it is one line from the paywall and nobody else owns it: Vaultify/Features/Subscription/LooxAcquisitionPaywallView.swift:189-190 uses bare English literals `Link("Terms of Use", ...)` and `Link("Privacy Policy", ...)`. Those auto-extract to Localizable.xcstrings, but per the project's own mandatory-localization rule they need VI and JA values before ship. Belongs to the iOS cluster.

UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS FOR THE OWNER.
- Is a Japanese App Store localization actually planned for this submission? If yes, P0-02 becomes blocking and jumps ahead of everything except P0-01.
- Should the analytics/crash default flip from on to off, or should the copy change? Changing the default (SettingsStore.swift:238-239) makes most of P0-03 true again and is a smaller diff than rewriting eleven strings in three languages — but it is a product decision with revenue-analytics consequences and I am not going to make it for you.
- What legal entity, address and governing law go into the terms? Nothing in either repo names them, and P0-04 cannot be completed without that answer.
- docs/fe-cloudflare-spec.md:42 says cron cleanup is "maintenance only" and docs/seo-content-plan.md marks "Permanently deleted" as do-not-use because cleanup was not enabled. Is the Loox Link cleanup cron live today? The retention section of the new privacy policy hangs on that answer, and I could not verify it from either repo.

findings.claim: Release packaging/signing is unsafe because VaultifyAutoFillMac (a macOS appex sharing bundle id com.bervion.vaultify.autofill with the iOS extension) can be built into / embedded in the iOS App Store archive.
findings.evidence: Project.swift:138-147 declares all three appex dependencies with platform conditions: `.target(name: "VaultifyAutoFill", condition: .when([.ios]))`, `.target(name: "VaultifyAutoFillMac", condition: .when([.macos]))`, `.target(name: "VaultifySafari", condition: .when([.ios]))`. Tuist materialises these as real pbxproj platform filters — Vaultify.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj:395 `VaultifyAutoFillMac.appex in Embed Foundation Extensions ... platformFilters = (macos, )`, :220 and :1106 carry `platformFilter = ios` for the Safari/iOS appexes; the PBXTargetDependency entries at :5570-5575 (platformFilters = macos) and :5579-5582 (platformFilter = ios) match. Empirically confirmed on the built product: /tmp/vaultify-dd/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/Vaultify.app/PlugIns contains exactly `VaultifyAutoFill.appex` and `VaultifySafari.appex` — no VaultifyAutoFillMac.appex. Signing is also consistent: fastlane/Matchfile lists only the three iOS identifiers (com.bervion.vaultify, .autofill, .safari) and fastlane/Fastfile force_manual_signing is called only for APP_TARGET/EXT_TARGET/SAFARI_TARGET. APS_ENVIRONMENT resolves correctly too (project.pbxproj:5993 development / :6059 production, from Project.swift:44-47), so the `$(APS_ENVIRONMENT)` entitlement in Vaultify/Vaultify.entitlements is not a TestFlight push trap.
